pageTitle: Morse - The Decentralized Headless CMS Protocol
heading: What is Morse?
text: Morse lets developers build content applications - blogs, knowledge bases, gated media platforms - where the backend is an open protocol instead of a vendor service. You define content structures, set access policies, and publish through a CLI or TypeScript SDK; the contracts handle identity, permissions, and revision history so there is no central point of failure to trust or migrate away from.

heading: Core Concepts
text: Understand the fundamental building blocks of the Morse protocol - the data model, authorization system, storage strategy, and how on-chain and off-chain components interact.

heading: The Data Model
text: Morse organizes content in a four-level hierarchy. Each level is stored on-chain and has a clear responsibility: Level 1 Publication → e.g. my-blog - a brand-level content domain Level 2 Collection → e.g. articles, site-pages - content lanes Level 3 Entry → e.g. welcome-post - a single content unit Level 4 Revision → immutable snapshot - blob reference + metadata

heading: A Concrete Example
text: Imagine you run a team blog. Here's how it maps to the Morse data model: Publication team-blog - your brand-level content domain, registered with a unique slug Collection articles - one content lane for blog posts (blob mode, since each post is independent) Entry #0 welcome-post - your first blog post, assigned the monotonic ID 0 Revision 0 - the initial published version. public_head points here, so readers see it immediately Revision 1 - an updated draft. draft_head points here, but public_head still points to revision 0 - readers see the original until you explicitly promote the draft Edito

heading: Publications
text: Think of a publication as your project or site - it is the top-level namespace that groups all your content together. Every publication gets a unique slug (like my-blog) that acts as a human-readable identifier across the protocol. All collections, entries, and permissions live under this single umbrella. See Publications for the full reference →

heading: Collections
text: Collections are how you organize entries within a publication - similar to folders or content types. For example, a blog might have an articles collection and a site-pages collection. When you create a collection, you choose how its content is stored: individually as separate blobs (good for standalone posts or images) or as a shared document that can be patched in place (good for structured data like settings or configuration). See Collections for the full reference →

heading: Entries & Revisions
text: Entries are the actual content pieces - a blog post, an image, a page. Every edit creates a new revision rather than overwriting the previous one, giving you a complete version history that can never be lost. The system tracks two pointers for each entry: a draft head for work-in-progress and a public head that readers see. This lets drafts evolve privately while production clients serve stable published content. See Entries for the full reference →

heading: How Publishing Works
text: End-to-end flow when you publish content: Authenticate - hold a PublisherCap for the target publication Upload - upload content bytes to Walrus, get a blob reference Register - create an entry on-chain storing the blob reference, content type, and access policy Heads update - public_head and/or draft_head update based on encryption status Read - any client resolves the entry and fetches the payload from Walrus

heading: Capability-Based Authorization
text: Instead of usernames and passwords, Morse uses on-chain capability objects to manage permissions. Owning the right object in your wallet proves you have permission to act - no login server required. Morse separates ownership from publishing using two types of capability tokens. An OwnerCap (one per publication) controls administrative operations like issuing permissions and deleting the publication. PublisherCaps (many per publication) grant write access and are bound to a specific holder address. Revocation uses a denylist-based model - issuing caps is cheap (zero table writes), and only revo

heading: Walrus Storage
text: The Sui blockchain only stores references (pointers) to your content, not the content bytes themselves. The actual payloads live on Walrus, a decentralized storage network designed for large data. This separation keeps on-chain costs low while ensuring your content is permanently available and verifiable. Walrus is format-agnostic, so Morse can support JSON, Markdown, images, video, or any custom schema. See Collections → Storage Modes for storage mode details →

heading: Access Control
text: Morse can gate content behind on-chain encryption using Seal. Only users who meet specific on-chain conditions can decrypt and read the content. This means access rules are enforced by the blockchain itself, not by a server you have to trust. This approach enables paid subscriptions, token-gated access, team-only content, and other models - all without a centralized gatekeeper. See Access Control for the full reference →

heading: Off-Chain Services
text: The blockchain is the canonical source of truth, but off-chain services improve the developer experience. Morse provides optional infrastructure like an indexer (for fast search and queries) and a content API (for read access) so you do not have to query the chain directly. These services make building apps on Morse faster and simpler, but they are not required. heading: Publications
text: A publication is the top-level permission management and identity boundary for a content domain in Morse. Everything - collections, entries, permissions - lives inside a publication.

heading: What is a Publication?

heading: The Slug System
text: Every publication is identified by a slug - a short, lowercase string that becomes its canonical identifier across the protocol. Slugs are enforced to be globally unique by the PublicationRegistry.

text: RuleConstraint CharactersLowercase letters a-z, digits 0-9, hyphens - Length1 to 64 characters Edge hyphensCannot start or end with - UniquenessMust be globally unique while the publication is active ImmutabilityCannot be changed after publication creation Examples // valid slugs "my-blog" "acme-corp" "docs2025" // invalid slugs "-leading-hyphen" // ESlugInvalidEdgeHyphen "trailing-hyphen-" // ESlugInvalidEdgeHyphen "UPPERCASE" // ESlugInvalidChar "spaces not allowed" // ESlugInvalidChar "" // ESlugEmpty

text: When a publication is deleted, its slug is released from the registry and becomes available again. This is a deliberate tradeoff - it gives publishers flexibility to re-register slugs - but teams should be aware that a released slug can be re-claimed by anyone.

heading: Collections
text: A collection is a named content lane inside a publication. It groups related entries together and determines how their Walrus payload references are stored.

heading: What is a Collection?
text: Collections organize entries into predictable buckets for editorial workflows and API consumers. A publication holds collections in a VecMap<String, Collection> keyed by name. The choice of VecMap reflects the expectation that a publication will have only a small number of named collections. Move public struct Collection has store { name: String, storage_mode: u8, // 0 = blob, 1 = quilt; immutable after creation next_entry_id: u64, // monotonic counter entries: Table<u64, Entry>, }

heading: Storage Modes
text: Every collection has a storage_mode set at creation that controls how entry revisions reference Walrus content. mode 0 Blob Mode Each entry revision references a standalone Walrus Blob object by its Sui object ID. mode 1 Quilt Mode Each entry revision stores a 37-byte QuiltPatchId pointing to a patch within a shared Walrus Quilt blob.

heading: Blob Mode
text: In blob mode, every revision stores a BlobRef::Blob(ID) - the Sui object ID of a standalone Walrus Blob. Each entry revision is fully independent: uploading new content creates a new blob, and the old blobs remain accessible by their IDs. Best for: Articles, blog posts, documentation pages Media libraries (images, videos, audio) Any collection where entries change independently and frequently Situations where you want maximum operational simplicity

heading: Quilt Mode

heading: Entries & Revisions
text: An entry is a single content unit within a collection. Revisions are its immutable history. The dual-head model lets drafts evolve freely while production readers always see a stable published state.

heading: Entry Structure
text: Entries live inside collections, stored in a Table<u64, Entry>. They have store and drop abilities - they are values owned by their collection, not independent Sui objects. Move public struct Entry has store, drop { name: String, revisions: vector<EntryRevision>, draft_head: Option<u64>, // index into revisions public_head: Option<u64>, // index into revisions } The name field must be non-empty and at most 256 characters.

heading: Revisions
text: Each revision is an immutable snapshot of an entry at a point in time. Revisions are never mutated after creation - edits always append new revisions to the vector. Move public struct EntryRevision has store, drop { blob_ref: BlobRef, // Walrus content reference content_type: String, // MIME type (e.g. "application/json") encrypted: bool, access_policy: u8, // 0=public, 1=publisher, 2=subscription seal_id: Option<vector<u8>>, // required when encrypted=true author: address, // tx sender at time of write } The content_type field must be non-empty and at most 255 characters; standard MIME format

heading: The BlobRef Enum
text: BlobRef is a Move enum that abstracts the two storage modes (the SDK surfaces it as a discriminated union - switch on .kind): Move public enum BlobRef has copy, drop, store { Blob(ID), // Sui object ID of a standalone Walrus Blob QuiltPatch(vector<u8>), // 37-byte QuiltPatchId } The variant used must match the collection's storage mode. The make_blob_ref function enforces this - you cannot accidentally mix modes.

heading: The Dual-Head Model
text: Every entry maintains two independent head pointers into its revision vector: draft_head Points to the latest draft revision. Work in progress - not visible to public readers. May be None on a freshly-published entry. public_head Points to the currently published revision. Stable for readers. May be None on an entry that has only drafts. revisions: [rev0, rev1(draft), rev2(draft), rev3(public), rev4(draft)] ↑ public_head=3 ↑ draft_head=4 This is what makes real editorial workflows possible: editors can keep appending drafts while production clients continuously serve the stable public_head.

heading: Adding an Entry
text: Create a new entry and add it to a named collection. Requires a valid PublisherCap. Returns the assigned entry_id. An entry cannot exist outside of a collection - every entry is scoped to exactly one. CLI SDK Move The --file flag provides the content; --content-type is inferred from the file extension if omitted. --epochs controls Walrus storage duration (defaults to 3). bash Copy morse entry add <name> --file <path> [--content-type <type>] [--epochs <n>] example Copy echo '{"title":"Welcome","body":"Hello, Morse!"}' > welcome.json morse entry add "welcome-post" --file ./welcome.json --content

heading: Access Control
text: Morse uses a capability-based permission model. Two types of capabilities control who can administer a publication and who can write content - enforced on-chain by the Sui type system, with no off-chain authorization service.

heading: Overview
text: Every write operation in Morse requires presenting a valid capability object. Capabilities cannot be fabricated - they can only be created by the protocol through designated functions. The type system itself is the enforcement mechanism. OwnerCap Admin authority. One per publication. Required to issue and revoke publisher caps, delete the publication, and transfer ownership. has key PublisherCap Write authority. Many per publication. Required for all content operations: create/delete collections and entries. Bound to a specific holder address. has key

heading: Ownership vs holder binding
text: A PublisherCap has two layers of authorization that must both be satisfied: Sui object ownership - which wallet physically holds the cap object. This determines who can pass it into a transaction. holder binding - an address set permanently at issuance. The contract checks cap.holder == ctx.sender() on every write operation. Both must match for the cap to work. Transferring a cap to someone who is not the bound holder gives them the object, but the contract will still reject their writes.

heading: Under the hood
text: When you issue a cap via the CLI or SDK, two Move calls are bundled in a single transaction: issue_publisher_cap creates the cap and binds it to the holder address. transfer_publisher_cap delivers the cap object to that address. No table write occurs during issuance - only revocations write to the denylist. This makes issuing caps essentially free beyond the gas cost of object creation.

heading: The Denylist Model
text: Morse uses a denylist (blocklist), not an allowlist, for publisher cap tracking. This is a deliberate design choice: Denylist (Morse)Allowlist (alternative) Issue capZero table writesOne table write per issuance Revoke capOne table writeOne table delete Write validationOne table lookupOne table lookup Optimized forCommon case (no revocations)Frequent churn This is safe because PublisherCap has no store ability and no external constructor - caps cannot be forged outside the module. An attacker cannot create a valid-looking cap; they must obtain a real one from the owner.

heading: Seal Integration
text: Morse integrates with Seal - Mysten's on-chain access control layer - to gate decryption of encrypted entry payloads. The integration is implemented via an entry fun that Seal calls during the decryption approval flow.

heading: CLI Overview
text: morse-cli is the command-line client for the Morse decentralized CMS. It signs with a locally encrypted key, stores content on Walrus, and encrypts private entries with Seal: the same protocol surface as the SDK, driven from your terminal. Runs on Node or Bun, pre-release on testnet. Published on npm · testnet only Install @arcadiasystems/morse-cli from npm. The CLI is currently configured for testnet only. Mainnet support to be added soon.

heading: Installing
text: The published binary is a Node-targeted bundle. You need Node (>= 18) or Bun (>= 1.2) to run it. bash Copy npm i -g @arcadiasystems/morse-cli morse --help Also available via bun add -g or pnpm add -g. Or run without installing: bash Copy npx @arcadiasystems/morse-cli --help

heading: Getting Started
text: Select an active publication and collection once - all subsequent commands will use them automatically, so you never have to paste a 64-character object ID. publication create and collection create auto-select the new object. See CLI Cookbooks for step-by-step guides.

heading: Active Context
text: The active publication and collection live in the current profile. Override per command with -P, --publication <slug|id> and -C, --collection <name>. Slugs resolve against publications owned by the active account. morse use <slug|id> [collection]: set the active publication and collection (optional) morse use --clear: clear the active context morse status: show the active profile, account, publication, and collection

heading: Security Model
text: Private keys are stored in an encrypted keystore (scrypt + AES-256-GCM) and unlocked by a password. Keys are never accepted as command-line flags. They come only from an interactive hidden prompt, the MORSE_PRIVATE_KEY env var, or the encrypted keystore. Keystore files are written chmod 600; group- or world-readable key files are refused on read. Keys are never printed or logged, including under --debug. The sole exception is account export, which deliberately reveals a key: interactive-only, requires confirmation, unavailable in --json. For CI, set MORSE_PRIVATE_KEY (raw key, never persisted)

heading: Configuration
text: Settings resolve with the precedence flags > MORSE_* env > config file > defaults. The config file lives under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/morse (default ~/.config/morse); encrypted keystores live in keystores/ beside it. VariableOverridesNotes MORSE_PROFILE-p, --profileProfile to use. heading: Output & Scripting
text: Human-readable output goes to stdout; progress, warnings, and prompts go to stderr. Redirecting stdout yields only the result. In --json mode, bigint values (e.g. gasUsedMist) are encoded as decimal strings and byte arrays (sealId, quilt patch IDs) as 0x-hex. Color is emitted only to a TTY and honors NO_COLOR / FORCE_COLOR. See CLI Command Reference → Global Options for a full list of global flags (--json, --quiet, --yes, and more).

heading: Publishing a New Revision
text: Append a new public revision directly, or stage a draft first and promote it. Revisions are append-only - existing revisions are never edited in place. Two heads track progress: draftHead (work in progress) and publicHead (the live version).

heading: Option A: Publish direct
text: Skip the draft stage and append a new public revision in one step. This updates publicHead immediately. bash Copy echo "hello morse, edited" > post.md morse revision publish-direct 0 --file post.md

heading: Option B: Draft then publish
text: Stage a draft revision first (updates draftHead only), then promote it to a public revision. By default, publish-from-draft reuses the draft's content; pass --file to replace it with new content. Useful when you want to review before going live. bash Copy echo "hello morse, draft" > draft.md morse revision append-draft 0 --file draft.md morse revision publish-from-draft 0 1 See also: SDK Cookbooks → Publishing a New Revision

heading: Delegating Write Access
text: Morse separates ownership (OwnerCap) from publishing (PublisherCap). The owner issues a cap bound to a co-author's address, granting them write access. Once issued, the co-author can publish entries using their own key. Revoking the cap causes further writes to abort on-chain. See Access Control -> Issuing Publisher Caps for details. As the owner, issue a cap to grant write access and revoke it to remove access: bash Copy morse cap issue 0xCO_AUTHOR_ADDRESS morse cap revoke 0xCAP_ID As a cap holder, list your caps or permanently destroy a specific cap: bash Copy morse cap list morse cap destro

heading: Transferring Ownership
text: The owner can transfer the publication's OwnerCap to another address, handing over full governance: the recipient becomes the new owner and can issue, revoke, and manage caps. bash Copy morse publication transfer-ownership 0xNEW_OWNER One-way for the sender Once transferred, the original owner loses all governance rights immediately. The new owner could transfer back, but there is no built-in undo. See also: SDK Cookbooks → Transferring Ownership

heading: Deleting and Tearing Down
text: Deletion is bottom-up: remove entries first, then collections, then the publication. Each container must be empty before it can be deleted. Entry IDs are permanently retired on deletion and never reused. See Entries → Deleting an Entry for details. bash Copy morse entry delete 0 morse entry delete 1 morse collection delete posts morse publication delete See also: SDK Cookbooks → Deleting and Tearing Down

heading: What PTBs Give You
text: Full transaction control Compose multiple Move calls in a single PTB - create a publication, add a collection, and publish an entry atomically. No SDK abstraction layer Call the contract functions directly. Useful when the SDK doesn't expose a wrapper for your use case or when you need fine-grained control. Custom batching Delete 50 entries, 3 collections, and a publication in one transaction. The SDK processes these sequentially; PTBs batch them. BCS encoding Pass Option<vector<u8>> and other Move types directly via @mysten/sui/bcs. Required for encrypted entries and quilt patches.

heading: Known Limitations
text: No encrypted publish path. publish_from_draft and publish_direct hardcode encrypted = false. Encrypted content stays as drafts - see Entries → Adding an Entry for the full lifecycle. Only the Publisher access policy is enforced. The Subscription policy constant is defined but the approval entry point is not yet implemented. All blobs must be deletable. The contract calls blob.is_deletable() and aborts if a permanent blob is passed. Single entry point module. All public functions live in publication::publication. The other modules are internal.

heading: Adding an Entry
text: Upload content to Walrus first, then pass the resulting Blob object ID to add_entry_to_collection. The blob argument is a reference to a Walrus Blob Sui object (&Blob), not a blob ID hash. Only deletable blobs are accepted. heading: Delegating Write Access
text: The owner issues PublisherCap objects to grant write access to co-authors. Revocation adds the cap ID to an on-chain denylist; all subsequent writes using that cap abort with EPublisherCapRevoked. See Access Control for the full capability model.

heading: Issuing a PublisherCap
text: Only the OwnerCap holder can issue new caps. The cap's holder field is fixed at issuance - the bound address is what grants write rights, not object ownership. typescript Copy const PUBLICATION_ID = "0xPUBLICATION_ID"; const OWNER_CAP_ID = "0xOWNER_CAP_ID"; const HOLDER_ADDRESS = "0xCO_AUTHOR_ADDRESS"; const tx = new Transaction(); // issue_publisher_cap returns the new PublisherCap. const newCap = tx.moveCall({ target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::issue_publisher_cap`, arguments: [ tx.object(PUBLICATION_ID), tx.object(OWNER_CAP_ID), tx.pure.address(HOLDER_ADDRESS), ], }); // Transfer the cap

heading: Deleting and Tearing Down
text: Deletion is strictly bottom-up. The Move layer enforces this: delete_collection calls table::destroy_empty on the entries table and aborts if any entries remain. delete_publication calls collections.destroy_empty() and aborts if any collections remain. Entry IDs are permanently retired on deletion and never reused.

heading: Troubleshooting
text: Move aborts surface as MoveAbort errors in the RPC response with a module name and numeric code. The table below maps the most common codes to their cause. CodeErrorModuleCause 6 ESlugAlreadyExists publication A publication with that slug already exists in the registry. 2 EUnauthorized publication The cap's publication_id does not match the publication object passed in the call. 4 EPublisherCapWrongHolder publication The transaction sender does not match cap.holder. 5 EPublisherCapRevoked publication The cap ID is on the publication's revoked denylist. heading: Glossary
text: Terms used throughout the Morse protocol and this documentation.

heading: A
text: Access Policy A numeric constant stored per revision that defines who can read the payload. Current values: 0 (public), 1 (publisher), 2 (subscription, reserved). Strictly coupled with the encrypted flag: public (0) requires encrypted=false; publisher (1) requires encrypted=true.

heading: B
text: Blob Mode Storage mode 0 for collections. Each entry revision stores a BlobRef::Blob(ID) pointing to an independent Walrus Blob object by Sui object ID. Best for growing, frequently-changing collections. BlobRef A Move enum stored per revision that abstracts the two Walrus payload reference formats. Variants: Blob(ID) for standalone blobs, QuiltPatch(vector<u8>) for 37-byte quilt patch identifiers.

heading: C
text: Capability A Move object that proves authorization to perform a specific action. Morse has two capability types: OwnerCap (admin authority) and PublisherCap (write authority). Capabilities cannot be fabricated - they can only be issued by the protocol. CMS Content Management System. Software for creating, organizing, and publishing structured digital content. Morse implements a decentralized, headless CMS protocol where permission management lives on-chain rather than in a centralized backend. Collection A named content lane inside a publication. Holds entries in a table keyed by monotonic ent

heading: D
text: dCMS Decentralized Content Management System - the category Morse belongs to. Publication identity, authorization, and state transitions are governed on-chain; payloads are stored off-chain in decentralized storage (Walrus). Denylist The revocation model used for PublisherCaps. A Table<ID, bool> on each publication stores IDs of revoked caps. Issuance writes nothing to the table; only revocations write. This optimizes for the common case where revocations never occur. Draft Head An Option<u64> pointer in an Entry that tracks the index of the latest draft revision. May be None if no draft has b

heading: E
text: Entry A single content unit within a collection. Holds a name, an immutable revision vector, and two head pointers. Identified by a stable monotonic entry_id within its collection. Entry ID A u64 assigned to an entry when added to a collection. Values start at 0 and increment monotonically. IDs are never reused after deletion - stable for external references. EntryRevision The Move struct that stores a single revision's data: blob_ref, content_type, encrypted, access_policy, seal_id, and author. Has store, drop abilities. Stored in an entry's revisions vector. Epoch A Walrus storage duration u

heading: G
text: gRPC A high-performance RPC framework used by SuiGrpcClient from @mysten/sui/grpc. The Morse SDK requires gRPC transport for all Sui interactions. Works in modern browsers without a proxy. See SDK Overview → Known Limitations for JSON-RPC fallback status.

heading: H
text: Headless CMS A CMS architecture that separates content management from presentation. The CMS manages content and metadata; client applications decide how to render it. Content is delivered through APIs. Morse follows this model while decentralizing identity, authorization, and state transitions. Holder The address field on a PublisherCap that binds the capability to a specific wallet. Write operations check that tx.sender() == cap.holder. A cap cannot be shared between addresses.

heading: I
text: Indexer The off-chain service that listens to on-chain events and builds a read-optimized index of publications, collections, and entries. Currently planned. See How Morse Works → Off-Chain Services.

heading: M
text: Monotonic ID A collection-scoped, auto-incrementing integer assigned to each entry. IDs are never reused after deletion. See Entries → Entry IDs. Move The programming language used for smart contracts on the Sui blockchain. Morse's on-chain logic is written in Move.

heading: O
text: OwnerCap The admin capability for a publication. Exactly one exists per publication. Grants authority to issue and revoke publisher caps, delete the publication, and transfer ownership. Has key ability only - transferable via transfer_owner_cap.

heading: P
text: Publication The top-level Morse content domain. A shared Sui object that bundles a name, an immutable slug, named collections, and a revocation denylist. Created via new_publication. PublicationRegistry A shared singleton Sui object created at package deploy time. Maintains a Table<String, ID> that maps slugs to publication IDs, enforcing global slug uniqueness. Required argument for new_publication and delete_publication. Public Head An Option<u64> pointer in an Entry that tracks the index of the currently published revision. What reader-facing clients should read. Updated by publish_collecti

heading: Q
text: Quilt Mode Storage mode 1 for collections. Each entry revision stores a 37-byte QuiltPatchId pointing to a patch within a shared Walrus Quilt blob. Best for stable, grouped content sets. QuiltPatchId A 37-byte identifier used in quilt mode collections. Layout: quilt_blob_id (32 bytes) || version (1 byte) || start_index (2 bytes) || end_index (2 bytes). Stored as a BlobRef::QuiltPatch(vector<u8>).

heading: R
text: Revision An immutable version of an entry at a point in time. Stored in the entry's revisions: vector<EntryRevision>. Each revision records a BlobRef, content type, encryption state, access policy, optional Seal identity, and author address. Revisions are never mutated - edits append new ones. Revision ID The index of a revision within an entry's revisions vector. Starts at 0. Returned by all revision-appending functions. Used to reference a specific revision in publish_collection_entry_from_draft. Revocation The act of adding a PublisherCap's object ID to a publication's denylist via revoke_p

heading: S
text: Seal Mysten Labs' on-chain access control layer for Walrus blob decryption. Morse integrates via the seal_approve_publisher entry function, which validates that an active publisher cap holder is authorized within a specific publication namespace. Seal Identity A byte vector (vector<u8>) that Seal presents to the approval function during decryption. In Morse, the format is: [publication_id (32 bytes)][policy_tag (1 byte)][nonce (variable)]. Scopes decryption approval to a specific publication and policy. Shared Object A Sui object accessible to any transaction, not owned by a single address. In

heading: T
text: Table A Sui framework type (sui::table::Table) used by Morse for dynamic key-value storage within on-chain objects. For example, collections store entries in a Table<u64, Entry>.

heading: W
text: WAL The utility token of the Walrus decentralized storage network. WAL is used to pay for blob storage and is separate from SUI (the gas token for Sui transactions). Walrus MystenLabs' decentralized blob storage network integrated with Sui. Morse stores all content payloads in Walrus - the contracts hold references (BlobRef), not the raw bytes. Walrus is format-agnostic; payload interpretation is the client's responsibility. Walrus Blob A Sui object (walrus::blob::Blob) representing a payload stored in the Walrus network. heading: Use Morse with AI
text: Morse publishes its documentation in machine-readable formats and ships agent-operable tooling, so AI coding agents can learn the protocol from current context — and then run the entire backend themselves.

heading: Machine-Readable Docs
text: Every page on this site is available in three agent-friendly forms. No scraping, no HTML parsing — just Markdown. Format URL Use it for llms.txt /llms.txt Compact index of all pages with one-line descriptions. Point an agent here first so it can pick which pages to read. llms-full.txt /llms-full.txt The complete documentation concatenated into a single Markdown file. One fetch gives an agent everything. Markdown twins /<page>.md Every page has a Markdown version at the same URL with .md instead of .html — e.g. /entries.md.

heading: Prime a Coding Agent
text: Paste one line into your agent to load the full Morse context: prompt Copy Read https://morsecms-docs.vercel.app/llms-full.txt — the full documentation for Morse, the decentralized headless CMS protocol on Sui + Walrus. Use it to help me build with the Morse CLI, TypeScript SDK, or Move contracts. Or fetch context on demand from a terminal-capable agent: bash Copy # Index of all pages curl -s https://morsecms-docs.vercel.app/llms.txt # One specific page as Markdown curl -s https://morsecms-docs.vercel.app/quick-start-cli.md # Everything at once curl -s https://morsecms-docs.vercel.app/llms-ful

heading: Copy Any Page for AI
text: Each docs page has a Copy page button (top right of the content area) with four actions: Copy page as Markdown — puts the page's Markdown twin on your clipboard, ready to paste into any assistant. View as Markdown — opens the raw .md version in a new tab. Open in ChatGPT / Open in Claude — opens the assistant with a prompt that references this page and the full docs. There is also Ask AI in the header (or press ⌘I): type a question and it opens Claude or ChatGPT pre-loaded with the entire Morse documentation as context.

heading: Agent-First by Design
text: Morse isn't just documented for agents — it is operable by them. There is no dashboard signup, no API-key console, no human-only provisioning step anywhere in the protocol.
